keyEvents.title: CLV cline and proto-Indo-Anatolian homeland
keyEvents.detail: Caucasus–Lower Volga (CLV) populations form a genetic cline mixing Caucasus hunter-gatherer–related, West Asian Neolithic, and steppe forager ancestries. 2025 Nature syntheses place the last shared speech community ancestral to Anatolian and core Indo-European among CLV people in this window. Bidirectional gene flow with Maikop-related Caucasus groups and Remontnoye-type steppe intermediates wires the pre-Yamnaya map. This is deep prehistory of language candidates—not Yamnaya inscriptions.

keyEvents.title: Late Trypillia megasites and Usatove contact
keyEvents.detail: Classic Cucuteni–Trypillia megasites of the forest-steppe flourish c. 4100–3600 BC and then wind down. Later, c. 3500–3000 BC, the Usatove group near the northwest Black Sea forms from a roughly even mix of steppe-related (CLV-derived) and Trypillian farmer ancestry, as North Pontic foragers, farmers, and pastoralists meet in overlapping pulses.

keyEvents.title: Yamnaya form from Serednii Stih on the Dnipro–Don
keyEvents.detail: Core Yamnaya crystallise as late Serednii Stih descendants after CLV migrants mix with Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer groups along the Dnipro–Don. Nikitin et al. 2025 highlight a genetically Yamnaya individual at Mykhailivka (3635–3383 BC) bridging the Eneolithic–Bronze Age gap at a likely formation epicentre. Explosive demographic growth follows after ~3750–3350 BC. Archaeological Yamnaya (~3300 BC) is the visible package of an older genetic fusion.

keyEvents.title: Kurgan pastoralism, wagons, and dairying take off
keyEvents.detail: Yamnaya groups bury under kurgans with ochre, weapons, and often wheeled vehicles—four-wheeled wagons as mobile pastoral gear on the Pontic–Caspian grass sea. Wilkin et al. 2021 show ruminant dairying becomes ubiquitous in dental-calculus proteomes at the Early Bronze Age onset, with horse-milk proteins in some individuals. Secondary products, not just meat, underwrite long-range mobility. The package links herds, milk, and wagon transport into an expansion engine.

keyEvents.title: Yamnaya expand to the Danube and Carpathian Basin
keyEvents.detail: By ~3000 BC Yamnaya-related horizons stretch from the Carpathian Basin and Hungary to Kazakhstan, with Danube–Hungary kurgans marking the western pastoral spearhead. Haak/Allentoft 2015 established this as the source of the later temperate-European ‘steppe’ ancestry pulse. Local farmer substrates (late Trypillia, GAC, Balkan Eneolithic) persist beside and under the expansion. The map is a gradient of contact, not an instant uniform coat.

keyEvents.title: Afanasievo leap to the Altai and Mongolia
keyEvents.detail: A genetically Yamnaya-related population appears far east in the Altai–Yenisei and even central Mongolia (Shatar Chuluu), carrying kurgan rites and early ruminant dairying. Afanasievo is the eastern twin of the Pontic expansion—same WSH package, different archaeology. It seeds later Inner Asian steppe histories and possible Tocharian-related linguistic models. Distance underscores how mobile Early Bronze Age pastoralism had become.

keyEvents.title: Globular Amphora hinge before Corded Ware
keyEvents.detail: West of the core steppe, Globular Amphora and late TRB farmer societies still dominate Central Europe while early steppe signals arrive patchily. GAC cattle-rich economies and distinctive amphorae sit on the hinge that will produce Corded Ware through Yamnaya-related admixture. France’s Late Neolithic already records early steppe pulses (~3000–2900 BC) ahead of full CW maps. The Copper Age west is still largely EEF+WHG when Yamnaya peaks on the steppe.

keyEvents.title: Two steppe pulses into Late Neolithic France
keyEvents.detail: Paris Basin collective burials (e.g. Bréviandes-les-Pointes) capture steppe ancestry arriving in real time: a Neolithic mother, a steppe-admixed son, and a reconstructed high-steppe grandfather. Science Advances 2024 models major admixture pulses ~3000/2900 BC (CW-linked) and ~2600 BC (Beaker-linked). France is a contact mosaic, not Britain’s cliff-edge replacement. Haplotypes show how families knit the new ancestry into local tombs.

keyEvents.title: Corded Ware explodes across the North European Plain
keyEvents.detail: Corded Ware appears by ~2900 BC (Bohemia and beyond) as a new cultural-genetic formation: Yamnaya-related steppe ancestry mixed with Globular Amphora–like farmers, not a pure Yamnaya clone. Single graves, cord-impressed beakers, and battle-axes replace many collective Neolithic rites. Papac et al. 2021 show early CW genetic diversity then sharp Y-chromosome bottlenecks toward R1a-M417. This is the main engine of temperate European Indo-Europeanization in standard models.

keyEvents.title: Single Grave Culture remakes Denmark
keyEvents.detail: Denmark’s second near-total Holocene turnover: Funnelbeaker farmers give way to Single Grave (Corded Ware) immigrants with high steppe ancestry. Allentoft et al. 2024 (100 Danish genomes) show parallel shifts in genotype, diet, and land use—SGC profiles already closer to present-day Danes. Earlier Gjerrild SGC genomes had previewed Yamnaya-derived ancestry. Pitted Ware coastal holdouts shrink as the new package spreads.

keyEvents.title: Battle Axe Culture enters Sweden
keyEvents.detail: Swedish Battle Axe (boat-axe) groups are the Scandinavian Corded Ware sister facies—steppe-rich, distinct from Funnelbeaker and Pitted Ware. Malmström et al. 2019 place BAC within the wider CW horizon, with more Neolithic farmer admixture than some early Baltic CW samples. Bergsgraven and related graves show new burial grammar: individual inhumations with polished stone battle-axes. Pre-Germanic speech models often start from this LNBA north.

keyEvents.title: Bell Beaker package spans western Europe
keyEvents.detail: Maritime and continental Bell Beaker pottery, wristguards, copper daggers, and archery kits spread from Iberia to Central Europe and the North Sea. Olalde et al. 2018 show Iberian and Central European Beaker people are genetically dissimilar—pots travel farther than people between those regions. Further north and west, migration matters more. Beaker is a prestige package riding different demographic engines.

keyEvents.title: Y-chromosome bottlenecks in CW and Beaker
keyEvents.detail: Bohemian aDNA shows Corded Ware Y-diversity collapsing to a dominant R1a lineage by ~2600 BC, then Bell Beaker Y-turnover around ~2400 BC with rising Neolithic-like ancestry. Social selection, patrilineal houses, or conquest demography—not neutral drift—best explain the simulations. Uniparental markers amplify a male-line story that autosomal ancestry only partly mirrors. Third-millennium Europe remakes kinship as well as pots.

keyEvents.title: Iberian Beaker keeps a stronger farmer base
keyEvents.detail: Unlike Britain, Iberian Beaker communities retain substantial EEF ancestry; steppe intake is more gradual and often male-biased. The same pottery fashion therefore maps opposite demographic stories on Atlantic vs North Sea shores. Later Iberian Bronze Age still sits on a higher-EEF ternary than post-Beaker Britain. Culture labels alone cannot predict replacement intensity.

keyEvents.title: Beaker Britain: ~90% population replacement
keyEvents.detail: The Beaker complex introduces high steppe-related ancestry and replaces ~90% of Britain’s Neolithic gene pool within a few centuries (Olalde et al. 2018). Y-haplogroup R1b rises from absent in Neolithic samples to >90% in Copper/Bronze Age Britain; new mtDNA lineages show women moved too. Continuity of monuments (e.g. Stonehenge landscapes) masks a demographic break. Island Britain becomes genetically closer to continental Beaker than to its own Neolithic farmers.

keyEvents.title: El Argar, Terramare, and Wessex regional BA
keyEvents.detail: Southeast Iberia’s El Argar builds fortified hill settlements and stark social hierarchy; Po Valley Terramare embank settlements; Britain’s Wessex culture raises rich barrows with continental metal links. Each rides the post-3000 BC ancestry mix with different EEF/steppe balances—Iberia keeps more farmer substrate than Britain. Regional Bronze Ages are parallel experiments, not one Nordic script.

keyEvents.title: Metal flood founds the Nordic Bronze Age
keyEvents.detail: Southern Scandinavia has little local copper; NBA wealth is imported. Nørgaard et al. 2021 track shifting ore sources: early British tin-bronze and Únětice-linked Alpine/Slovak copper, then Carpathian and later northern Italian metal after ~1500 BC. Continuous metal flow from ~2100–2000 BC fuels elite competition visible in weapons and ornaments. The NBA is a network society before it is a ‘local’ metallurgy.

keyEvents.title: Sintashta chariots and steppe war-tech
keyEvents.detail: In the southern Urals, Sintashta–Petrovka cemeteries bury the earliest clear horse-drawn spoked-wheel chariots beside fortified settlements and advanced bronze weaponry. Bayesian dating puts light chariots in the early 2nd millennium BC, transforming earlier Yamnaya wagon traditions. Related steppe ancestries and horse lineages feed later European and Near Eastern chariotry. Rock-art chariots farther west echo this pan-Eurasian prestige tech.

keyEvents.title: Srubnaya and eastern steppe BA continuity
keyEvents.detail: Timber-grave (Srubnaya) and related forest-steppe cultures maintain steppe-rich ancestry east of the Carpathians, on pathways often linked toward early Indo-Iranian. They parallel European BA diversification farther west without the Nordic rock-art package. Chariot and horse ideologies circulate across this continuum. Eastern Europe’s Bronze Age stays pastoral-steppe in flavour while temperate Europe farms and trades metal.

keyEvents.title: Nordic Bronze Age cultural climax
keyEvents.detail: Longhouse farms, thousands of burial mounds, ostentatious swords and lurs, and figurative rock art define a Scandinavian fluorescence on a gene pool already reset by Single Grave/Battle Axe. Genetically this is continuity, not a third total replacement after TRB and SGC. Amber exports and metal imports wire chiefs into European exchange. Pre-Germanic speech is the mainstream linguistic frame—reconstructed, not written.

keyEvents.title: Tumulus to Urnfield in Central Europe
keyEvents.detail: Middle Bronze Tumulus burial traditions give way to Late Bronze Urnfield cremation complexes across much of Central Europe. Ancestry largely stabilises the Corded Ware–derived ternary; culture names proliferate faster than genetic turnovers. Urnfield–Hallstatt arcs are often linked (debated) toward early Celtic ethnolinguistic formations. Cremation urnfields rewrite how communities remember the dead.

keyEvents.title: Mycenaean palaces and Linear B Greek
keyEvents.detail: Mycenaean palace societies write early Greek in Linear B—the first securely attested Indo-European language in Europe. Genomes show moderate steppe-related ancestry on an Aegean/Anatolian-farmer-rich base, far less steppe than Corded Ware Denmark. Northern Balkans join Carpathian–Danube BA networks while the Aegean runs a palace economy. Language here is epigraphic fact; steppe correlation remains model-dependent.

keyEvents.title: Amber routes reach the Aegean
keyEvents.detail: Baltic amber travels south and east toward Mycenaean Greece while metal and ideas move north—Kristiansen & Suchowska-Ducke’s ‘connected histories.’ After Únětice’s decline ~1600 BC, Nordic access to Carpathian copper and eastern routes intensifies. Elite graves and hoards track the same corridors as isotope-provenanced metal. The NBA is a northern node of a Bronze Age world-system, not an isolate.

keyEvents.title: Rock art ships, sun discs, and ritual landscapes
keyEvents.detail: Bohuslän, Østfold, Tanum, and inland Swedish panels carve fleets, warriors, ploughs, and sun symbols into coastal bedrock—visual ideology of a seafaring metal age. Ling, Kristiansen, and others link shoreline ship imagery to long-distance exchange; inland panels may mark aggregation and handover sites. The Trundholm sun chariot (Denmark) materialises the same solar cosmology in bronze. Ritual and trade share one iconography.

keyEvents.title: Edict of Nantes
keyEvents.detail: Henry IV's Edict of Nantes ends the French Wars of Religion by granting limited Huguenot worship and civil rights inside a Catholic kingdom—an uneasy confessional settlement that becomes the baseline for seventeenth-century France.

keyEvents.title: Thirty Years' War
keyEvents.detail: The Thirty Years' War wrecks Central Europe after the Defenestration of Prague: Bohemian revolt, Swedish and French intervention, and mass famine/disease empty German lands while Habsburg, Swedish, and Bourbon power collide.

keyEvents.title: Peace of Westphalia
keyEvents.detail: Peace of Westphalia (Münster & Osnabrück; Spanish–Dutch peace earlier that year) ends the German war, confirms Dutch and Swiss independence, extends Calvinist toleration, and hardens territorial sovereignty inside the Holy Roman Empire.

keyEvents.title: Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
keyEvents.detail: Louis XIV's Edict of Fontainebleau revokes Nantes; dragonnades and forced conversions drive roughly 150,000–200,000 Huguenots into exile toward the Dutch Republic, England, Brandenburg, and Switzerland—redrawing skilled Protestant diasporas across the map.

keyEvents.title: Glorious Revolution
keyEvents.detail: England's Glorious Revolution replaces James II with William III & Mary II; the 1689 Bill of Rights limits the crown and locks a Protestant succession that underpins later British parliamentary monarchy and Atlantic power.

keyEvents.title: Great Northern War
keyEvents.detail: The Great Northern War ends Swedish Baltic hegemony: after Poltava (1709) and the Treaty of Nystad (1721), Russia under Peter I gains Ingria, Estonia, and Livonia and becomes a European great power on the eastern map.

keyEvents.title: Industrial Revolution
keyEvents.detail: Industrialization begins in Britain (steam, textiles, coal/iron) then spreads to Belgium, the Rhineland, and northern France—urban factories, railways, and demographic surge remake Europe's economic geography before politics catches up.

keyEvents.title: French Revolution
keyEvents.detail: The French Revolution abolishes the Ancien Régime: Estates-General to National Assembly, rights declarations, republic, Terror, and Directory—exporting popular sovereignty and anti-feudal reform that unsettle every neighboring monarchy.

keyEvents.title: Congress of Vienna
keyEvents.detail: The Congress of Vienna (Final Act 9 June 1815) resettles Napoleonic Europe: France trimmed, a German Confederation under Austrian lead, Russian Poland, and a conservative balance of power meant to freeze borders for decades.

keyEvents.title: Revolutions and national unifications
keyEvents.detail: Nation-state consolidations crest: 1848 revolutions shake Habsburg and German lands; Italy unifies (1861; Rome 1870); Prussia's wars forge the German Empire (1871), replacing Vienna's German Confederation with a Berlin-centered map.

keyEvents.title: First World War
keyEvents.detail: World War I shatters the continental empires: after 1918, Austria-Hungary, German, Russian, and Ottoman realms collapse into successor nation-states under Versailles and related settlements—Europe's political map is redrawn in a few years.

keyEvents.title: Second World War and the Holocaust
keyEvents.detail: World War II and the Holocaust devastate the continent; Nazi Germany's conquest and defeat, followed by Soviet advance in the east, leave Europe occupied, partitioned, and demographically scarred on a scale unmatched in modern history.

keyEvents.title: Iron Curtain and two German states
keyEvents.detail: Cold War division hardens: Iron Curtain, occupation zones, and the 1949 birth of two German states (FRG/GDR) split Central Europe into NATO/Western and Soviet-bloc systems for four decades.

keyEvents.title: Treaties of Rome
keyEvents.detail: Treaties of Rome (25 Mar 1957; in force 1958) create the European Economic Community among Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands—the institutional core of later EU integration.

keyEvents.title: Fall of communism
keyEvents.detail: 1989 revolutions open the Berlin Wall (9 Nov); German reunification follows (3 Oct 1990); the Soviet Union dissolves (1991)—Eastern Europe's communist map collapses into independent nation-states oriented toward markets and, soon, EU/NATO.

keyEvents.title: Maastricht Treaty
keyEvents.detail: Maastricht Treaty (signed 7 Feb 1992; in force 1 Nov 1993) founds the European Union, EU citizenship, and the path to Economic and Monetary Union—renaming and deepening the Communities into today's political frame.

keyEvents.title: Euro and EU enlargement
keyEvents.detail: Euro notes and coins circulate (2002); the 2004 enlargement brings much of Central and Eastern Europe into the EU, aligning the political atlas with post-Cold War democracies from the Baltics to the Balkans' northern edge.

keyEvents.title: Hallstatt Iron Age begins
keyEvents.detail: Hallstatt C opens temperate Europe’s Iron Age: iron weapons and tools spread from Alpine/central workshops while elite tumulus burials revive warrior display.

keyEvents.title: Jastorf culture in the north
keyEvents.detail: Jastorf urnfield communities crystallize across northern Germany and Jutland—the main archaeological backdrop usually tied to early Germanic ethnolinguistic formation.

keyEvents.title: Greeks found Massalia
keyEvents.detail: Phocaean Greeks found Massalia (Marseille), anchoring Mediterranean wine, olive, and prestige-goods trade up the Rhône into Hallstatt elite networks.

keyEvents.title: Hallstatt princely seats
keyEvents.detail: Late Hallstatt princely seats (Fürstensitze) peak: Hochdorf, Vix/Mont Lassois, and peers bury Mediterranean imports that advertise alpine–Greek contact.

keyEvents.title: Roman Republic founded (traditional)
keyEvents.detail: Roman tradition dates the expulsion of the Tarquin kings and the birth of the Republic—later annalistic memory for a late-sixth-century shift away from Etruscan kingship.

keyEvents.title: Herodotus describes the Scythians
keyEvents.detail: Herodotus’s Scythian ethnography fixes Iranian-speaking steppe nomads as the Greek world’s northern foil, matching rich kurgan horizons north of the Black Sea.

keyEvents.title: Hallstatt collapse, La Tène rises
keyEvents.detail: Western Hallstatt hillfort elites collapse (Heuneburg destruction; Mont Lassois abandoned) as La Tène art and new warrior rites take over Celtic Europe.

keyEvents.title: Gauls sack Rome
keyEvents.detail: Senone Gauls defeat Rome at the Allia and sack the city—trauma that later Roman writers used to define the Celtic ‘barbarian’ threat.

keyEvents.title: Galatian invasion of Greece
keyEvents.detail: Brennus’s Galatians invade Macedonia and Greece and fail at Delphi, spawning the Soteria festival and locking Celts into Hellenistic sacred memory.

keyEvents.title: First Punic War
keyEvents.detail: First Punic War ends with Sicily as Rome’s first overseas province, launching Republican Mediterranean imperialism that soon engulfs Corsica, Sardinia, and Iberia.

keyEvents.title: Second Punic War
keyEvents.detail: Second Punic War: Hannibal’s Alpine invasion and Roman counter-conquest shatter Carthaginian power in Spain and Italy and make Rome western Mediterranean hegemon.

keyEvents.title: Carthage and Corinth destroyed
keyEvents.detail: Rome destroys Carthage and Corinth in the same year, annexing Africa and tightening grip on Greece—a brutal marker of mid-Republican expansion.

keyEvents.title: Caesar's Gallic Wars
keyEvents.detail: Julius Caesar’s Gallic Wars conquer the La Tène polities of Gaul; Vercingetorix’s revolt ends at Alesia (52 BC), opening mass Latinization of western Europe.

keyEvents.title: Actium and the Principate
keyEvents.detail: Actium (31) and Octavian’s settlement as Augustus (27) end the Republic’s civil wars and create the Principate that administers Europe’s Roman provinces.

keyEvents.title: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
keyEvents.detail: Arminius destroys three legions under Varus in the Teutoburg Forest, freezing the Rhine as Rome’s practical northern limit in Germania.

keyEvents.title: Roman conquest of Britain
keyEvents.detail: Claudius invades Britain under Aulus Plautius; Colchester falls and Britannia becomes a frontier province with towns, roads, and army bases.

keyEvents.title: Wielbark expansion
keyEvents.detail: Wielbark culture expands from Pomerania south and east along the Vistula–Bug, absorbing Przeworsk zones—the archaeological horizon standardly linked to early Gothic traditions before Pontic moves.

keyEvents.title: Chernyakhov culture
keyEvents.detail: Chernyakhov (Sântana de Mureș) culture crystallizes north of the Black Sea as a multiethnic Gothic-dominated horizon built on Wielbark traits plus Sarmatian and local elements.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Adrianople
keyEvents.detail: Hunnic pressure drives Goths across the Danube; at Adrianople (9 Aug 378) Fritigern’s Goths kill Emperor Valens—the worst Roman field defeat since Cannae and a hinge of late Roman crisis.

keyEvents.title: Visigoths sack Rome
keyEvents.detail: Alaric’s Visigoths sack Rome (24 Aug)—the first sack of the city in eight centuries—shocking Mediterranean opinion and hastening Gothic settlement politics in Gaul and Spain.

keyEvents.title: Wielbark networks collapse
keyEvents.detail: Wielbark settlement networks in Poland collapse archaeologically as Migration-Period upheaval empties much of the Odra–Vistula Germanic landscape before early Slavic expansion.

keyEvents.title: Adventus Saxonum (traditional)
keyEvents.detail: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle’s Adventus Saxonum: Hengest and Horsa invited into Britain; Angles, Saxons, and Jutes begin the North Sea settlement that remakes eastern England’s language and ancestry.

keyEvents.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
keyEvents.detail: At the Catalaunian Plains, Aëtius’s Romano-Visigothic coalition checks Attila’s Hunnic invasion of Gaul—one of the West’s last great coalition battles before Attila’s death (453).

keyEvents.title: End of the Western Empire
keyEvents.detail: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus in Italy, conventionally ending the Western Roman Empire as a separate imperial court while Eastern Rome continues from Constantinople.

keyEvents.title: Ostrogothic Italy
keyEvents.detail: Theodoric the Great’s Ostrogothic kingdom rules Italy from Ravenna under nominal imperial grant—Roman administration with a Gothic warrior elite until Justinian’s later reconquest wars.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Soissons
keyEvents.detail: Clovis defeats Syagrius at Soissons, ending the last Roman rump in northern Gaul and founding Merovingian Frankish kingship over a Gallo-Roman majority.

keyEvents.title: Baptism of Clovis
keyEvents.detail: Clovis’s baptism into Nicene Christianity (traditionally by Remigius at Reims) aligns the Franks with Gallo-Roman bishops—unlike Arian Gothic kingdoms—and becomes Merovingian origin myth.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Tours/Poitiers
keyEvents.detail: Charles Martel’s victory near Tours/Poitiers checks a major Umayyad raid from al-Andalus and cements Carolingian military prestige inside the Frankish realm.

keyEvents.title: Pepin founds the Carolingians
keyEvents.detail: Pepin the Short is anointed king of the Franks with papal backing, deposing the last Merovingian and launching the Carolingian dynasty.

keyEvents.title: Saxon Wars
keyEvents.detail: Charlemagne’s Saxon Wars forcibly integrate Saxony: mass baptisms, the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, and the 782 Verdun massacre mark brutal Christianization of the north.

keyEvents.title: Viking raids escalate
keyEvents.detail: Viking raids escalate from Lindisfarne (793) into overwintering armies and assaults on Frankish riverine towns (e.g. Paris 845), forcing fortification and tribute politics across the North Sea world.

keyEvents.title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
keyEvents.detail: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne emperor in Rome, inventing a Western imperial title that claims parity with Byzantium and frames Latin Christendom’s political theology.

keyEvents.title: Treaty of Verdun
keyEvents.detail: Treaty of Verdun partitions Louis the Pious’s empire among Lothar I, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald—West, Middle, and East Francia as durable templates for France and Germany.

keyEvents.title: Slavic mission and Bulgarian conversion
keyEvents.detail: Cyril and Methodius’s Slavic mission and Bulgaria’s conversion under Boris I pull Southeast Europe into Byzantine Christian literacy while Carolingian and papal spheres compete for the Slavs.

keyEvents.title: Normandy founded
keyEvents.detail: Charles the Simple grants Rollo land around the lower Seine (Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte), founding Normandy—a Norse duchy that will latinize yet keep North Sea martial habits.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Lechfeld
keyEvents.detail: Otto I’s victory over the Magyars at the Lechfeld secures East Frankish/Ottonian hegemony and clears the path to his imperial coronation (962).

keyEvents.title: Poland, Hungary and Rus' convert
keyEvents.detail: Piast Poland (Mieszko I’s baptism c. 966), Árpád Hungary (Stephen I crowned 1000/1001), and Vladimir’s Rus’ (988) enter Latin or Byzantine Christendom—millennium state formation on the European frontier.

keyEvents.title: Hugh Capet elected
keyEvents.detail: Hugh Capet is elected king of West Francia, opening the Capetian dynasty that slowly recentralizes France from the Île-de-France outward.

keyEvents.title: Iceland adopts Christianity
keyEvents.detail: Iceland’s Althing accepts Christianity by law; around the same years Norse voyages reach Greenland and Vinland—the farthest Atlantic edge of the Viking world.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Clontarf
keyEvents.detail: Battle of Clontarf: Brian Boru’s forces defeat a Dublin–Leinster–Norse coalition; Norse towns remain, but Irish high-kingship politics shift after Brian’s death in the aftermath.

keyEvents.title: Cnut's North Sea empire
keyEvents.detail: Cnut the Great rules a North Sea empire linking England, Denmark, and (for a time) Norway—the high-water mark of Scandinavian royal power in the British Isles.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Stiklestad
keyEvents.detail: Olaf Haraldsson falls at Stiklestad; his rapid cult as St Olaf becomes Norway’s conversion emblem and a royal-saint model for the north.

keyEvents.title: 1066: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
keyEvents.detail: Harald Hardrada dies at Stamford Bridge; weeks later William of Normandy wins at Hastings—ending Anglo-Saxon rule and conventionally closing the Viking Age in England.

keyEvents.title: Canossa and the Investiture Contest
keyEvents.detail: Investiture Contest climax: Gregory VII excommunicates Henry IV; the emperor’s penance at Canossa dramatizes the struggle over who names bishops in Latin Europe.

keyEvents.title: First Crusade
keyEvents.detail: Pope Urban II’s call at Clermont (1095) launches the First Crusade; Jerusalem falls in 1099 and Latin crusader states appear in the Levant.

keyEvents.title: Frederick Barbarossa
keyEvents.detail: Frederick I Barbarossa rebuilds imperial authority in Germany and Italy and dies leading the Third Crusade (1190)—emblem of Hohenstaufen ambition.

keyEvents.title: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
keyEvents.detail: The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople, founding the Latin Empire and permanently weakening Byzantium—a self-inflicted wound of Latin Christendom.

keyEvents.title: Albigensian Crusade
keyEvents.detail: The Albigensian Crusade devastates Cathar Languedoc and extends Capetian power into the south, tying heresy repression to French state-building.

keyEvents.title: Las Navas de Tolosa
keyEvents.detail: Christian Iberian kings crush the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa, opening the later 13th-century collapse of Muslim power in Iberia outside Granada.

keyEvents.title: Magna Carta
keyEvents.detail: English barons force King John to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede—a feudal peace charter that later generations remade into a liberty myth.

keyEvents.title: Mongol invasion
keyEvents.detail: Mongol armies smash Rus’ principalities and raid Poland and Hungary (Legnica and Mohi, 1241), imposing the Golden Horde’s long shadow on Eastern Europe.

keyEvents.title: Hundred Years' War
keyEvents.detail: The Hundred Years’ War between England and France—intermittent but transformative—produces Crécy, Poitiers, Agincourt, Joan of Arc, and the eventual French reconquest of Gascony.

keyEvents.title: Black Death
keyEvents.detail: The Black Death enters Europe via Black Sea and Mediterranean shipping (often tied to Caffa/Crimea) and kills roughly one-third to one-half of the population in the first pandemic wave.

keyEvents.title: Golden Bull
keyEvents.detail: Charles IV’s Golden Bull fixes the seven electors who choose the Holy Roman Emperor, constitutionalizing the Empire’s princely electoral order until 1806.

keyEvents.title: Western Schism
keyEvents.detail: The Western Schism splits Latin Christendom between rival popes at Rome and Avignon (later a third line), shattering papal prestige until the Council of Constance.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Kosovo
keyEvents.detail: Ottoman victory at Kosovo consolidates Turkish power in the Balkans and becomes a long Serbian historical memory of loss and martyrdom.

keyEvents.title: Battle of Grunwald
keyEvents.detail: Poland–Lithuania under Jogaila and Vytautas crush the Teutonic Order at Grunwald (Tannenberg), checking crusader-state power on the Baltic.

keyEvents.title: Agincourt and Joan of Arc
keyEvents.detail: Agincourt (1415) briefly resurrects English hopes; Joan of Arc’s 1429 Loire campaign and 1431 martyrdom reverse French morale toward eventual Valois victory.

keyEvents.title: Gutenberg's press
keyEvents.detail: Gutenberg’s movable-type press at Mainz begins European print culture—Bibles, indulgences, and soon Reformation pamphlets will travel at new speed.

keyEvents.title: Fall of Constantinople
keyEvents.detail: Mehmed II takes Constantinople with gunpowder artillery, ending the Byzantine Empire; the same year Castillon ends the Hundred Years’ War in France’s favour.

keyEvents.title: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses
keyEvents.detail: Martin Luther circulates the Ninety-Five Theses against indulgence abuses (traditionally said to be posted on the Wittenberg church door, a detail historians debate), the conventional spark of the Protestant Reformation in the Empire.

keyEvents.title: Diet of Worms
keyEvents.detail: At the Diet of Worms, Luther refuses to recant before Charles V; the Edict of Worms outlaws him, while print and princely protection spread his cause.

keyEvents.title: German Peasants' War
keyEvents.detail: The German Peasants’ War couples evangelical rhetoric with agrarian revolt; its crushing clarifies that magisterial Reform would ally with princes, not rural revolution.

keyEvents.title: Act of Supremacy
keyEvents.detail: Henry VIII’s Act of Supremacy makes the English monarch head of the Church of England, breaking Rome’s jurisdiction without yet fully Lutheranizing doctrine.

keyEvents.title: Calvin's Geneva
keyEvents.detail: John Calvin’s Geneva becomes the disciplined model of Reformed Protestantism; the Institutes and consistory discipline export a second Reformation to France, Scotland, and the Netherlands.

keyEvents.title: Council of Trent
keyEvents.detail: The Council of Trent defines Catholic doctrine, reform, and discipline—the institutional spine of the Counter-Reformation against Protestant confessions.

keyEvents.title: Ivan IV crowned tsar
keyEvents.detail: Ivan IV is crowned first Tsar of Russia, asserting Orthodox autocracy just as Western Europe splinters by confession.

keyEvents.title: Peace of Augsburg
keyEvents.detail: Peace of Augsburg settles cuius regio, eius religio for Catholic and Lutheran estates in the Empire—freezing a bi-confessional map that excludes Calvinists until later wars.

keyEvents.title: Abdication of Charles V
keyEvents.detail: Charles V abdicates, splitting Habsburg power between Philip II’s Spanish-global monarchy and Ferdinand’s Austrian imperial line—Europe’s defining dynastic geometry at mid-century.

keyEvents.title: Post-glacial Maglemosian wetlands boom
keyEvents.detail: As ice sheets retreated and deciduous forest spread, Maglemosian and related foragers densified around lakes, rivers, and coastal wetlands from Britain to southern Scandinavia and the North European Plain. Bone and antler leister points, dugout canoes, and microlithic toolkits mark a watery economy of fish, waterbirds, and red deer. Sites such as Star Carr (North Yorkshire) preserve timber platforms and ritualised deer-skull headdresses that show social display, not just subsistence. These WHG-related groups are the western baseline before farming.

keyEvents.title: Doggerland shrinks into North Sea islands
keyEvents.detail: Relative sea-level rise after the last glaciation gradually drowned the southern North Sea plain—Doggerland—fragmenting a once-continuous forager landscape into marshes, islands, and tidal flats. Mesolithic people tracked shifting coasts; submerged palaeolandscapes still yield flint and seismic river valleys under modern waters. By the late 7th millennium BC only remnant archipelagos remained. Britain’s separation from the continent was a multi-century drowning, not a single catastrophe.

keyEvents.title: Iron Gates foragers thrive on the Danube
keyEvents.detail: At the Iron Gates gorges (Lepenski Vir, Vlasac, Schela Cladovei), Mesolithic groups built trapezoidal riverside houses and buried people with elaborate rituals beside a fishery of migratory sturgeon and other fish. Their genomes sit on a WHG–EHG cline with distinctive local structure. Contact with incoming Anatolian-related farmers begins in the 7th–6th millennia BC, producing some of Europe’s earliest farmer–forager genetic mixtures. The gorge was a corridor, not a sealed refuge.

keyEvents.title: Atlantic and Baltic shell-midden economies
keyEvents.detail: Along Iberia’s Cantabrian coast, Brittany, and the future Ertebølle zone of southern Scandinavia, foragers piled shell middens that record intensive marine and estuarine harvesting. Stable isotopes often show heavy aquatic diets compared with inland forest hunters. These coastal packages persist as farmer frontiers advance, becoming classic ‘last forager’ holdouts in the north. Material culture stays microlithic and ceramic-free until contact zones introduce pottery.

keyEvents.title: 8.2 ka cold pulse hits Holocene foragers
keyEvents.detail: The 8.2 ka event—the sharpest Holocene cooling recorded in Greenland ice—brought decades of colder, often drier conditions across Atlantic and northern Europe. High-resolution shell middens such as El Mazo (Asturias) show seasonal sea-surface cooling and shifts in harvested shellfish. Northwest European radiocarbon syntheses argue for resilience and reorganization rather than continent-wide population collapse. The pulse likely intensified mobility just as farming approached the southeast.

keyEvents.title: Storegga tsunami slams North Sea coasts
keyEvents.detail: A massive submarine landslide off Norway triggered the Storegga tsunami (~8150 cal BP), sending multi-metre run-ups onto coasts from Norway and Scotland to the southern North Sea. Sediment sheets and a confirmed submarine deposit in Doggerland’s ‘Southern River’ valley prove the wave struck both land and drowned lowlands. It was probably not the final drowning of Doggerland—much was already underwater—but it was a sudden, lethal shock for coastal Mesolithic communities. Archaeological traces of human impact remain scarce relative to the geological signal.

keyEvents.title: WHG–EHG forager networks intensify
keyEvents.detail: Genome-wide data show that after ~8000 BC admixture between western Oberkassel/WHG-related and eastern Sidelkino/EHG-related foragers increased across temperate Europe. The cemetery of Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov (Karelia) samples a large EHG-related community with rich grave goods; western sites remain WHG-dominated. Scandinavian hunter-gatherers (SHG) sit on this cline with elevated eastern affinity. Climate stress and the approaching farmer frontier both likely drove forager mobility.

keyEvents.title: Eastern pottery foragers without farming
keyEvents.detail: East of the early farmer line, Narva, Comb Ware, and related groups adopt ceramics while remaining genetically hunter-gatherer for millennia. In Ukraine and the forest-steppe, ‘Neolithic’ often means pottery, not crops—genomes stay WHG–EHG without Anatolian farmer ancestry until much later. This ‘great divide’ between farmer west and forager east structures Europe until steppe expansions after ~3000 BC. It warns against equating pottery horizons with demic farming.

keyEvents.title: Anatolian-related farmers enter the Balkans
keyEvents.detail: Farming villages with domestic cereals, sheep/goat, and pottery appear in Greece and the central Balkans, carrying ancestry tightly related to northwest Anatolian Neolithic populations (EEF). Starčevo–Körös–Criș communities push into the Carpathian Basin by the early 6th millennium BC. Local hunter-gatherer admixture is initially limited in pioneer cores. This demic wave sets the genetic template for almost all later European farmers.

keyEvents.title: Two routes: Cardial coast vs LBK Danube
keyEvents.detail: From a shared Balkan-era farmer source, Neolithic packages split. Impressa/Cardial pioneers leapfrog the northern Mediterranean by sea, reaching Iberia by ~5500 BC with cockle-shell stamped pottery. In parallel, Linearbandkeramik (LBK) crystallises in Transdanubia and races up the Danube–loess corridor into Central Europe. Ancient genomes show both streams share Anatolian-related ancestry despite different pottery styles. Culture labels track routes; the people are cousins from one meta-population.

keyEvents.title: LBK longhouses carpet Central Europe
keyEvents.detail: LBK settlements of timber longhouses, cattle-rich economies, and banded pottery spread from the Paris Basin to Ukraine within a few centuries. Cemetery-scale aDNA (Polgár, Nitra, Asparn-Schletz and others) shows patrilocality—more male than female within-site relatives—and systematically higher WHG ancestry in eastern than western LBK. Pioneer farmers were socially structured, not a genetic monolith. Loess soils and river corridors structured the map.

keyEvents.title: Cardial maritime pioneers reach Iberia
keyEvents.detail: Cardial groups establish littoral farming enclaves from Liguria and Provence to Catalonia, Valencia, and Atlantic Portugal. The Cova Bonica (Barcelona) Cardial genome clusters with other early European farmers and Sardinians, with a forager signature not simply local Iberian WHG. Rapid coastal radiocarbon patterns fit maritime pioneer colonisation better than slow land diffusion. Inland Mesolithic foragers persist beside the littoral farmer wedge for generations.

keyEvents.title: Farmer–forager contact west of the Rhine
keyEvents.detail: Genome-wide data from France show higher local Loschbour-like WHG ancestry in early Neolithic groups west of the Rhine than in classic Central European LBK. Admixture timing often precedes the archaeological ‘contact’ phase by many generations, implying prolonged, uneven mixing. Sites such as those near the Paris Basin and Mediterranean hinterland record pottery and burial diversity at the frontier. Farming advanced as a porous frontier, not a clean replacement everywhere.

keyEvents.title: Vinča tells and Balkan village florescence
keyEvents.detail: Across the central Balkans, Vinča and related tell settlements accumulate deep strata of houses, fine dark pottery, and early copper ornaments. Population packing on tells contrasts with the dispersed LBK longhouse pattern farther north. These communities remain EEF-dominated genetically while experimenting with metallurgy and long-distance exchange. They anchor the southeast while Central Europe’s first farmers reorganise after the LBK.

keyEvents.title: Ertebølle and northern forager holdouts
keyEvents.detail: While LBK farmers occupy loess belts, Ertebølle communities of southern Scandinavia and the southwest Baltic keep a coastal hunting–fishing–gathering life with pointed-base pottery and rich middens. Genetically they remain SHG/WHG-related until Funnelbeaker farming centuries later. Similar holdouts (Narva, Comb Ware) persist farther east. The Early Neolithic map is a farmer core ringed by durable forager arcs.

keyEvents.title: Late LBK massacres: Talheim to Schletz
keyEvents.detail: At Talheim (Germany), Asparn-Schletz (Austria), and Schöneck-Kilianstädten (Germany), mass graves document blunt-force and arrow killings of whole communities near the end of the LBK. Kilianstädten adds systematic lower-limb breakage suggesting torture or mutilation; young adult women are underrepresented at some sites, hinting at capture. aDNA from Schletz shows victims drawn from a large population, not a tiny kin band. Collective violence was a repeated late-LBK feature, not a one-off myth.

keyEvents.title: Herxheim: ritual destruction of bodies
keyEvents.detail: The double-ditched enclosure at Herxheim (Rhineland-Palatinate) received the carefully smashed remains of hundreds of people—skull caps, defleshed bone, destroyed pots and tools—over a relatively short late-LBK window. Consensus has shifted from a single massacre toward repeated, highly standardised ritual processing, possibly including cannibalism. Strontium hints that many victims were non-local. It is a crisis of rite and meaning as much as of warfare.

keyEvents.title: WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer Europe
keyEvents.detail: After centuries of EEF dominance, Middle Neolithic genomes from Iberia, France, Germany (e.g. Baalberge), and elsewhere show rising hunter-gatherer ancestry—often toward ~15–30% regionally, higher on Atlantic façades. Y-chromosome lineages of Mesolithic I2 type become common in farmer men, implying male-mediated forager gene flow. Britain is a noted exception with little post-arrival WHG rebound. Culture stayed ‘Neolithic’ while the gene pool quietly re-indigenised.

keyEvents.title: Atlantic megaliths ignite in northwest France
keyEvents.detail: Passage graves, cairns, and standing-stone alignments emerge in Brittany and Normandy (Barnenez, early Carnac landscapes) before spreading along Atlantic and western Mediterranean façades. Northern France sits at the genetic and cultural hinge of Cardial-related and Danubian farmer traditions. Later work links megalith spread to regions touched by Cardial-related ancestry and to trade networks that outlasted the founding migrations. Monumentality becomes the period’s signature architecture.

keyEvents.title: Early Trypillia expands across the forest-steppe
keyEvents.detail: Precucuteni–Early Trypillia groups push rapidly through Moldovan and Ukrainian forest-steppe in the 47th–45th centuries BC, founding painted-pottery villages between the Prut and Dnieper. AMS chronologies show fast dispersal with overlapping stylistic phases rather than a slow ripple. Genetically these farmers remain in the EEF world while neighbouring steppe and forest foragers stay distinct. Eastern Europe gains a dense village belt facing the Pontic steppe.

keyEvents.title: Michelsberg, Chasséen, and enclosure Europe
keyEvents.detail: Michelsberg (Central Europe) and Chasséen (France) reorganise post-LBK landscapes with ditched enclosures, new flint extraction, and broader exchange. WHG ancestry continues to climb in many of these Middle Neolithic farmer groups compared with Early Neolithic pioneers. Regional identities multiply even as monumental and enclosure practices rhyme across western Europe. The loess world after LBK was plural, not a single successor culture.

keyEvents.title: Funnelbeaker opens the northern frontier
keyEvents.detail: The Funnelbeaker/TRB complex brings agriculture, megalithic tombs, and new pottery into southern Scandinavia and the north European plain, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle foragers unevenly. Early TRB farmers are still mostly EEF-derived but with elevated northern HG ancestry. Causewayed enclosures and flint mines (e.g. Belgium–Denmark axis) signal regional aggregation. The north finally joins farmer Europe—centuries after the loess belt.

keyEvents.title: Carnac, Morbihan, and Breton stone theatres
keyEvents.detail: The Morbihan and Carnac regions host extraordinary densities of menhir alignments, tumuli, and jadeitite ceremonial axes exchanged from Alpine sources. Elite tumulus burials and broken axe deposits point to competitive ritual economies, not anonymous peasant religion. Armorica becomes a western magnet for exotic stone and maritime contacts. These landscapes remain among Europe’s densest prehistoric monument fields.

keyEvents.title: Trypillia megasites: Europe’s first mega-towns
keyEvents.detail: Aggregated settlements over 100 ha—and megasites up to ~320 ha with perhaps 10–15,000 people—appear northwest of the Black Sea (Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki and peers). Isotope food-webs show pulse-heavy, heavily manured cropping plus fenced cattle pastures that supplied dung—an integrated ‘mega-economy.’ Decline after ~3650 BC looks social and political more than purely ecological. These were the world’s largest settlements before Mesopotamia’s fame.

keyEvents.title: Farming crosses to Britain and Ireland
keyEvents.detail: Continental farmers introduce cereals, cattle, rectangular houses, and funerary monuments to Britain and Ireland around the turn of the 4th millennium BC; secure Irish house-and-cereal horizons cluster ~3720–3680 BC. aDNA shows a first near-replacement of insular Mesolithic WHG by EEF-related newcomers. Causewayed enclosures, portal tombs, and early passage graves follow within generations. This is the islands’ first great genetic turnover—Beaker will be the second.

keyEvents.title: Orkney, Boyne, and Atlantic tomb florescence
keyEvents.detail: Maeshowe-type tombs and settlements such as Skara Brae in Orkney, and the Boyne Valley passage tombs (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth) in Ireland, push megalithic architecture and astronomical alignments to a Late Neolithic climax. Communities remain EEF-rich with regionally variable WHG; steppe ancestry has not yet arrived. Grooved Ware networks tie the Irish Sea and northern Britain into a shared ceremonial world. Monument time peaks just before the Corded Ware–Beaker genetic storm.

keyEvents.title: Pitted Ware foragers beside TRB farmers
keyEvents.detail: On Scandinavian coasts, Pitted Ware groups renew a marine-mammal and fish-focused hunting life with distinctive pottery while Funnelbeaker farmers occupy inland soils. Their genomes retain high HG ancestry relative to neighbouring farmers—an archaeological culture that is also a genetic holdout. Seal hunting and island cemeteries (e.g. Ajvide, Gotland) define the package. Farmer Europe still had forager neighbours at its northern edge.
